The citation itself survives every attack: I fetched the Project Gutenberg text (ebook 2701) and read the whole first paragraph of chapter 1, Loomings. The retained wording is exact for the 1851 text, including the semicolon after 'grim about the mouth' and the comma in 'then, I account it high time'. The verifier's correction of the opening capital is right: 'Whenever I find myself growing grim about the mouth' does begin its own sentence, immediately after 'driving off the spleen and regulating the circulation.' The locator is right (it is the opening paragraph, which runs from 'Call me Ishmael' to 'the same feelings towards the ocean with me'); the attribution is right; Ishmael is correctly named as the speaker; the work is correctly given as the Harper and Brothers 1851 American edition, which is the one titled 'Moby-Dick; or, The Whale' (the London Bentley issue was 'The Whale'); the tag Fiction is the form of the work; the source line leads with the name, carries no dash, and runs 123 characters. shipped.js returns no match, no near-opening, herman melville at 0 of 3, not banned. Nothing on the misattribution list touches it.

I refute on two grounds that are not the citation.

FIRST, THE NOTE IS FACTUALLY WRONG ABOUT ITS OWN ELLIPSIS. The note says 'The ellipsis marks the elided clauses about coffin warehouses and funerals.' It does not. The ellipsis swallows three clauses, and the longest of them is the one the note never mentions: 'and especially whenever my hypos get such an upper hand of me, that it requires a strong moral principle to prevent me from deliberately stepping into the street, and methodically knocking people's hats off'. That is the clause standing immediately before the 'then' the quotation resumes at, so the note misdescribes precisely the join it exists to explain. Roughly sixty words are cut and twenty-five kept; a note that accounts for a third of the cut and calls it the cut is a confident false statement in a track whose whole standard is that a confident false statement is worse than an honest one.

SECOND, PUBLISHABILITY AND MONTH. The sentence quoted is not freestanding. Melville glosses it two sentences later, in the same paragraph: 'This is my substitute for pistol and ball.' The paragraph's own account of going to sea is that it is what Ishmael does instead of shooting himself, and the elided hypos clause is the ramp into that gloss. As printed the card needs no content warning, so it passes rule 11 on its face, but a reader who follows the locator meets one in the next line, and the note says nothing. Rule 3 also bites: July is Courage in Trial, and this is a melancholy-and-escape line, the impulse to leave rather than to hold. Its natural home is a month about voyages, not a month about enduring. 'Damp, drizzly November in my soul' at six in the morning is the bleakness rule 3 excludes, carried by an ellipsis that hides the reason it is bleak.

WHAT WOULD FIX IT. The citation needs no change. Either rewrite the note to state the full elision and Melville's own gloss, and accept that the card then reads as a voyage line rather than a courage line, or take the uncut famous opening instead. If the editor wants Melville in July, 'Call me Ishmael.' is clean, uncut, needs no ellipsis and no note, and is the sentence the work is known by: Herman Melville, Moby-Dick; or, The Whale, chapter 1, Loomings, the opening sentence (Ishmael) (Harper and Brothers, 1851), 121 characters. I have not put that in betterCitation because it is a different line, not a better citation of this one.
